name: Facial feminization surgery

card.summary: A set of bone and soft-tissue facial operations developed for transgender women, now eyed by some looksmaxxers for brow, nose and cheek work.
card.note: Evidence is from transgender patient cohorts; use for appearance goals in cisgender men is untested.

quick.overview:
Facial feminization surgery is a group of operations that soften masculine facial features: lowering the hairline, shaving the brow ridge, reshaping the nose, building up cheeks, and reducing the chin, jaw and Adam's apple.

It was developed in the 1980s by Douglas Ousterhout for transgender women. Reviews report improved quality of life and a low complication rate, though the studies are mostly case series. On looksmax.org, a few users discuss borrowing its techniques for male faces.
quick.mechanism: Surgeons plan from CT and MRI imaging and then reshape bone (brow ridge, chin, jaw), soft tissue (nose, lips, brows), and add volume to cheeks with implants or fat. Operations are large and may be staged or combined.
quick.risks: Reported risks include nerve injury, infection, implant displacement, fat resorption, bone-healing problems after forehead work, and vocal changes after tracheal shave. These are major operations under general anaesthesia and costs can be high; coverage depends on country and insurer.

lead: Facial feminization surgery (FFS) is a group of reconstructive procedures that change typically masculine facial features toward more typically feminine proportions. It is performed mostly for transgender women and other transfeminine people, and covers the hairline, forehead and brow ridge, nose, cheeks, lips, chin, jaw and the thyroid cartilage (Adam's apple).[1][2] The visual effect is a softer forehead and brow, a smaller and more refined nose, fuller cheeks, a shorter upper lip and a narrower lower face.[5][8]

Its techniques come from craniofacial, ear-nose-throat and plastic surgery. Douglas Ousterhout is credited with developing most of the procedures from the early 1980s.[1][2] Surgeons plan from imaging, and procedures can be done together in a single long operation or in stages.[1][11]

Published research on FFS is largely about quality of life and gender dysphoria in transgender patients. A prospective international multicenter cohort followed patients before and after surgery and reported changes in a facial feminization outcome score, and reviews describe improved well-being with low complication rates.[1][4]

In looksmaxxing communities, some users look at FFS as a source of techniques, for example brow bone reduction, nose reshaping and cheek work, to change the eye area and facial width in cisgender men who want a softer or more harmonious face.[3]

chain: Brow, nose, cheek, lip, chin and jaw are reshaped surgically
Facial proportions move toward feminine norms
angle.text: FFS physically reshapes the bone and soft tissue of the face, so the change in appearance is direct and permanent. Some looksmaxxers borrow individual procedures, such as brow bone shaping or cheek augmentation, to alter how masculine or heavy a male face looks.[3]

infobox: Gender dysphoria related to facial appearance[4]
Hairline, brow bone, rhinoplasty, cheeks, lip lift, chin and jaw, tracheal shave[1][6]
Tens of thousands of dollars for extensive work, per Grokipedia[2]

paras: Surgeons commonly use CT and MRI imaging to identify features and plan the operation, and procedures are grouped by thirds of the face.[1]

The hairline can be lowered, advanced or restored with transplant grafts. The brow ridge can be shaved down or, where the frontal sinus lies behind it, reshaped and refixed (cranioplasty). A brow lift can reposition the eyebrows, and orbital reconstruction can change eye socket shape.[1] Wikipedia notes that data do not clearly favour one method of ridge reduction over another and that results data on orbital work are limited.[1]

Rhinoplasty for transfeminine patients reduces nose size and reshapes the tip and bridge; reviewers note it shares its technical basis with rhinoplasty in cisgender patients but is planned around feminine proportions.[5][6][7] Cheeks can be built up with implants or fat grafts and a lip lift shortens the upper lip.[1][5]

Chin length can be reduced by shaving or a sliding genioplasty, and the jaw angle and masseter muscle can be reduced; one published technique removes a sagittal section of the mandible from the angle toward the mental nerve region, usually combined with genioplasty.[1][8] A chondrolaryngoplasty (tracheal shave) reduces the Adam's apple while preserving laryngeal function.[9][10]

Wikipedia lists risks by procedure: nerve injury (mental nerve damage being the main concern in chin and jaw work), tooth root injury, infection, bone non-union, implant displacement, resorption of grafted fat, impaired nasal valve function, bone-healing problems after forehead work and vocal cord injury after tracheal shave. It describes overall complication rates as low and notes many can be corrected with further surgery.[1][10] A 2024 study examined soft-tissue complications after FFS bone surgery.[13] Grokipedia, which is AI-generated, reports complication rates of 5 to 25 percent across studies and attributes the spread to uneven reporting.[2]

Reviews of preparation describe patients researching extensively online, medical clearance and, commonly, a supporting letter from a mental health professional.[1][11] Separate reviews discuss timing of FFS relative to other gender-affirming care and relative to hair and other treatments.[12]

In 1982 Darrell Pratt, a surgeon performing genital reassignment surgery, asked Douglas Ousterhout to operate on a transgender woman whose face still drew male-gendered reactions. Ousterhout, who had reconstructed faces affected by birth defects and trauma, studied early twentieth-century anthropology and cephalometric measurements to define femininity and tested his measurements on skulls.[1] His 2009 book on the topic is cited as a foundation of the field.[1] Later reviews describe the field as growing worldwide and still evolving in technique.[6][14]

Coverage varies. Wikipedia reports that insurers commonly cover FFS in France, Belgium and the Netherlands, that coverage is difficult to obtain in Germany, and that in the United States coverage has increased since the Affordable Care Act.[1] An editorial in the Journal of Craniofacial Surgery discusses how surgeons and patients define what counts as feminine in facial planning.[15]

Grokipedia raises questions about causal effects on dysphoria, notes research on social perception in which some post-FFS faces were rated as less attractive and more masculine than cisgender female faces, and cites reports of regret. These claims are attributed to that AI-generated source.[2]

A prospective international multicenter study of gender-diverse adults with gender dysphoria compared a facial feminization outcome score before and after surgery, at one week to one month and after more than six months, alongside photogrammetric measures.[4] A 2016 systematic review by Morrison and colleagues concluded FFS can improve well-being and quality of life with a low complication rate, and a 2017 review by Berli and colleagues recommended its inclusion in guidelines as medically necessary.[1] A 2010 study by Ainsworth and Spiegel found mental-health quality of life lower in transgender women with no surgery than in those who had genital surgery, FFS or both, and Spiegel (2011) concluded the forehead and upper third had more influence on gender perception than the lower jaw or midface.[1] Grokipedia reports short-term satisfaction above 80 percent and limited long-term data.[2] No published study has tested these procedures for appearance goals in cisgender men.

timeline.event: Douglas Ousterhout operates on a transgender woman at the request of surgeon Darrell Pratt, beginning the development of FFS.[1]
Ousterhout publishes a guide to FFS for transgender women.[1]
Morrison and colleagues publish a systematic review of FFS outcomes.[1]
Berli and colleagues review the evidence and recommend inclusion in guidelines.[1]
First prospective international multicenter quality-of-life study published.[4]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, FFS appears as a source of techniques for men who feel their faces look heavy-browed or masculine; participants discuss it alongside implants and other surgical options.[3]

claims.claim: FFS techniques such as brow bone shaping and cheek augmentation can remove an 'ogre' look and improve harmony in a male face.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org poster says brow shaping softens a heavy eye area, cheek augmentation can fix facial width and rhinoplasty can address the nose, citing before-and-after patient images, while avoiding brow lifts that give a surprised look.[3]
claims.experts: Published FFS research concerns outcomes in transgender patients; no published study tests these procedures for appearance goals in cisgender men.[1][4]

claims.claim: A full FFS-style approach costs more than cheek implants plus limited reshaping, and many implants on an underdeveloped face may look unnatural.
claims.believers: A reply argues that a full set of implants (brow, jaw, cheek) would cost more than cheek implants plus limited reshaping.[3]
claims.experts: Grokipedia reports full FFS costs in the tens of thousands of US dollars; no source compares costs for this use.[2]
